issues.legal_issue: An unregistered agreement to transfer immovable property executed after the registration requirement took effect may be received as evidence of a contract in a suit for specific performance, but not to obtain protection of possession through part performance.
material_facts: The plaintiff relied on an unregistered agreement to sell executed after the registration requirement took effect in a suit seeking specific performance.
The agreement was offered as evidence of the contract, and the trial court had not decided its genuineness, validity, or binding effect.
issues.conclusion: The agreement could be received as evidence of the contract in the specific-performance suit under the proviso to Section 49 of the Registration Act, but it could have no effect for the purposes of Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act. Its genuineness, validity, binding nature, and any other statutory objections remained for the trial court to decide after evidence was adduced.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 17(1A) and 49 of the Registration Act, 1908, read with Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, require registration of a post-commencement contract when it is relied on for protection under Section 53A; non-registration removes that effect but does not prevent the document from being received as evidence of a contract in a specific-performance suit under the proviso to Section 49. The Court applied S. Kaladevi v. V.R. Somasundaram, (2010) 5 SCC 401, which restated the principles in K.B. Saha and Sons Private Limited v. Development Consultant Limited, (2008) 8 SCC 564.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and contract_document_unregistered and contract_document_executed_after_registration_requirement and document_offered_as_contract_evidence

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A party brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract concerning immovable property.
predicates.contract_document_unregistered: The party relied on a document containing a contract to transfer immovable property that was not registered.
predicates.contract_document_executed_after_registr: The contract document was executed after the registration requirement for reliance on possession protection had taken effect.
predicates.document_offered_as_contract_evidence: The party offered the document as evidence of the contract in the specific-performance suit.

issues.definition: When an unregistered post-requirement contract document is offered as contract evidence in a specific-performance suit, it may serve as contract evidence but not as a basis for possession protection.

issues.legal_issue: A registered power of attorney should not be rejected at the document-admissibility stage on a stamp-duty objection founded on incorporation of a referenced agreement; the stamp and other statutory questions may be decided after evidence is adduced.
material_facts: A registered power of attorney had been executed in favour of one defendant and referred to an earlier agreement to sell.
The plaintiff, who relied on the power of attorney, was not a party to it.
The trial court considered the power of attorney receivable as evidence and left questions about its legal effect and statutory compliance open for decision after evidence.
The High Court treated the power of attorney as given for consideration by incorporating the terms of the referenced agreement and ruled it inadmissible for insufficient stamp duty.
issues.conclusion: The trial court was justified in treating the registered power of attorney as carrying a rebuttable presumption that it had been duly stamped and in leaving the statutory questions for decision after evidence. The High Court should not have resolved the stamp-duty objection by construing the referenced agreement as incorporated into the power of attorney. The question of impounding an insufficiently stamped instrument remained open for the trial court at the appropriate stage.
issues.legal_principle: A registered document gives rise to a rebuttable legal presumption that it has been duly stamped. Questions about whether the instrument is affected by the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, or the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, may be determined after oral and documentary evidence. Avinash Kumar Chauhan v. Vijay Krishna Mishra, (2009) 2 SCC 532, concerns the court’s power to impound an insufficiently stamped instrument under Section 35 of the Indian Stamp Act; that issue remained open for the trial court. The Court also held that the High Court should not have applied incorporation by reference in this setting, where the plaintiff relying on the power of attorney was not a party to it.

rule.if: appeal_over_document_admissibility and registered_power_of_attorney and stamp_objection_based_on_referenced_agreement and evidentiary_record_not_yet_adduced

predicates.appeal_over_document_admissibility: A party appealed a ruling made before trial evidence was completed about whether documents could be received as evidence.
predicates.registered_power_of_attorney: A party relied on a registered power of attorney executed in favour of another person.
predicates.stamp_objection_based_on_referenced_agre: An opposing party claimed that the power of attorney attracted greater stamp duty because it referred to an agreement whose terms were said to be incorporated into it.
predicates.evidentiary_record_not_yet_adduced: The parties had not yet adduced the oral and documentary evidence relevant to the instrument’s statutory compliance and legal effect.

issues.definition: When a registered power of attorney is challenged on a stamp objection based on a referenced agreement before the relevant evidence has been adduced, it is not rejected at that preliminary stage on that objection.

issues.legal_issue: An agreement to transfer immovable property executed before the registration requirement took effect is not subject to that requirement, and may in any event be received for a limited evidentiary purpose in a specific-performance suit.
material_facts: An agreement to sell was executed before the statutory registration requirement for contracts relied on under the part-performance provision took effect.
The agreement was referred to in a registered power of attorney and was among the documents offered in the specific-performance suit.
issues.conclusion: The earlier agreement was not required to be compulsorily registered under the later requirement. Even if registration were required, it could be received as evidence for a limited purpose, without effect for the purposes of Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17(1A) of the Registration Act, 1908, applies prospectively. Under Section 49 of that Act, an unregistered document may be received as evidence of a contract in a specific-performance suit or of a collateral transaction not requiring a registered instrument, while it has no effect for the purposes of Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. The Court applied S. Kaladevi v. V.R. Somasundaram, (2010) 5 SCC 401, and the principles discussed in K.B. Saha and Sons Private Limited v. Development Consultant Limited, (2008) 8 SCC 564.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A party brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract concerning immovable property.
predicates.contract_document_executed_before_regist: The contract document was executed before the statutory registration requirement for reliance on possession protection took effect.
